Municipal governments in cities such as Baltimore County, Maryland; Jacksonville, Florida; and Austin, Texas, reported being unable to send or receive emails, though emergency services like 911 were not impacted. According to the note's midday ET update on November 13, availability was improving, but intermittent issues persisted, and Microsoft had not given a restoration time. At that point, Microsoft had reported no evidence of malicious activity, and the root cause was still under investigation.

It was the resignation heard across the world. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the company for 33 years, had officially stepped down. “It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news. Over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor, pouring tens of billions into startups annually, and participating in 105 rounds this year alone often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook. “If that direction changes, it’ll be a big blow to so many young companies,” said Maria Davidson, founder of Relational Capital. Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition. “Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Dawn Capital’s Shamilla Bankiya told TechCrunch. Most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures. Padval has known Huang since serving on the board of Mellanox Technologies, a networking chipmaker Nvidia acquired for approximately $7 billion in 2020. While there is hope that Huang’s eventual successor will resume his dealmaking spree, investors aren’t hopeful that it will happen in the short term.

Luxembourg Prime Minister Luc Frieden insisted that Europe must take its fate into its own hands. “We cannot let neither the Americans nor the Russians decide about our future,” Frieden said. A global Microsoft outage disrupted Outlook, Teams, Copilot and other Microsoft 365 services, affecting businesses, government agencies, healthcare services and law enforcement across several countries. The global reach of the outage was swift. After problems first emerged midday Thursday in the U.S., online tracker Downdetector said it received outage reports from 74 countries and territories within an hour. Story continues below this ad The total number of people affected was not clear, but Microsoft said in January it had more than 450 million paid commercial subscriptions to its 365 services. Microsoft said a technical issue arose during an upgrade that followed “a recent network change.” The company added that it restored services gradually, which took longer. As Microsoft addressed issues affecting its Exchange Online mailboxes, it earlier cited a failure that it said caused a number of its servers to be “unexpectedly unavailable” during automated checks. Story continues below this ad For Outlook, many users said they couldn’t send and receive emails, or had trouble loading their inboxes altogether. Those problems piled up across much of the world into Friday. By Friday morning in the U.S., Microsoft said email queues were “significantly reduced and approaching normal levels.” Still, it warned of potential intermittent access and ongoing delays. On Thursday, the company said it had “successfully restored” Microsoft Teams in North America, although some users continued to report connectivity issues.

text:
New French protests focus on children and police

France is experiencing widespread protests against inflation and a new police bill, with high schools and citizens taking part in demonstrations as elections approach.
Follow Paris, France: France faces more rallies on Saturday with demonstrators venting frustrations ranging from inflation to opposition to a new police bill at the latest protests. The European Union’s second largest economy has been gripped by high-school blockades and cost-of-living demonstrations for more than a month, ahead of presidential elections next year that the far right sees as its best chance of seizing power. Some of the largely peaceful rallies have seen fringe violence, as well as accusations of police brutality. People were to take to the streets for the fifth Saturday in a row, with a main rally in Paris from 1:00 p.m. (1200 GMT) and dozens of other gatherings across the country. In the capital, the Yellow Vest movement would join high-school students, unions and other activists fighting for children’s rights or opposed to a bill to give police more protection in their use of weapons. “Society’s in bad shape,” said Claire Bourdille, from a collective battling violence against children and teenagers. “We can’t focus on one cause more than another.” Activists have in recent months demanded better protection for children against sexual abuse. Others will be protesting against a new bill in parliament to grant police who use their weapons a presumption of legitimate self-defense. Backers, including the far-right National Rally party of presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen, say it is necessary to avoid police being automatically suspected of using disproportionate force. ‘Licence to kill’ Activists argue the bill, approved by the lower house and soon to go to the Senate, amounts to a “license to kill.”

France Protests: Student Demonstrations, Riots and Macron's Response | Outlook India

France protests over school conditions and living costs escalated into nationwide riots. Here's how student demonstrations, police clashes and public anger challenged Macron's government. - Demonstrations escalated into nationwide unrest on October 17, with clashes, looting and allegations of excessive police force. - Protests continued in November over education, wages and living costs, putting pressure on Emmanuel Macron's government. France has witnessed weeks of protests, school blockades, clashes with police, arson and looting as demonstrations over deteriorating educational facilities, rising living costs and government spending cuts escalated into nationwide unrest. On October 17, hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets, with largely peaceful demonstrations overshadowed by violent clashes, attacks on public buildings and the looting of businesses in several cities. The movement began with high school students demanding better school infrastructure, more teachers and improved learning conditions. It subsequently drew support from trade unions, public-sector workers, Yellow Vest activists and others opposed to the government's economic policies. As the unrest spread, police tactics became another source of anger, while President Emmanuel Macron's government blamed far-left groups and criminal elements for the violence. How did the protests in France begin? The protests began on September 21 at Saint-Exupéry high school in Créteil, a suburb southeast of Paris, where several teaching positions were vacant. Students began blockading schools over teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms, deteriorating buildings and demanding improvements to their school schedules. Related Content

Microsoft restores service to Outlook and Teams after global outage Downdetector logs over 7.4m reports worldwide, highlighting global dependence on Microsoft's workplace tools --- Reuters November 14, 2026 4 min read facebook twitter whatsup linkded email Photo: REUTERS --- Microsoft said on Saturday that services had fully recovered across Teams, Outlook and its other products, ending a global outage that crippled online communications for businesses and governments for over 24 hours. "We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions," the company posted on X. The outage, reports of which started climbing around 1725 GMT on Thursday according to Ookla, is one of the longest in Microsoft's history and the second disruption to its services this year. Microsoft said the outage specifically hit features tied to Exchange Online — its cloud-based email and scheduling hub — leaving unconnected applications operational. The incident deepens questions about the global reliance on a handful of Big Tech companies that supply both the essential software and the cloud infrastructure that underpins it. It also highlighted the dependence on Microsoft's workplace software, with outage reports spiking as employees began their workdays across Asia and Europe, according to Downdetector's parent company, Ookla. Downdetector logged more than 7.4 million reports worldwide, peaking at nearly 20,000 a minute, more than 1,500 times normal levels. "It shows how much of the working day now runs through one provider's email and collaboration tools," said Luke Kehoe, lead industry analyst at Ookla. Disruptions and financial losses from the outage could ​result in numerous insurance claims, but the overall hit to insurers is expected to be limited, said Mario De Cicco, vice president of European financial institutions at Morningstar DBRS. 4 Several airlines reported disruptions to their email support services. Microsoft Resolves 36-Hour Global Outage Affecting Outlook, Teams Insurance losses estimated at $300M-$500M as outage disrupted global businesses, gov Microsoft Resolves 36-Hour Global Outage Affecting Outlook, Teams Insurance losses estimated at $300M-$500M as outage disrupted global businesses, governments, and critical sectors By Park Ji-youn(ChosunBiz) Published 2026.11.14. 19:48Updated 2026.11.14. 20:02 On October 26, the Microsoft building in Washington State, USA. /Reuters-Yonhap Microsoft’s global outage affecting its business programs, including Outlook and Teams, was fully resolved after 36 hours. The prolonged disruption of essential services such as email, calendar management, and video conferencing caused widespread damage across businesses and government institutions worldwide. According to Reuters, Microsoft announced on the 14th (local time) around 6 a.m. GMT that it had fully restored its services, including Teams and Outlook. Microsoft stated via its MS365 X (formerly Twitter) account, “We have completed measures to address the root cause of this incident and have restored services for the remaining affected customers and regions.” The outage began around 5:25 p.m. GMT on the 12th, with reports surging rapidly. According to the global outage tracking site Downdetector, over 7.4 million cases were reported in more than 70 countries worldwide. At its peak, reports spiked to approximately 20,000 cases per minute, over 1,500 times the usual rate. This service disruption marks the second incident this year and is considered one of the longest outages in Microsoft’s history. Microsoft previously attributed the outage to server issues, particularly affecting functions related to Exchange Online, its cloud-based email and calendar service. Its AI assistant, Copilot, was also impacted, though no malicious external activity was detected.

Rachit Agarwal / Digital Trends Microsoft says it has finally restored its Microsoft 365 services after an outage that affected Outlook, Teams, Copilot, and other apps for more than a day. The company posted on X on Saturday, November 14, to confirm that services had been restored for the remaining affected customers and regions. The outage lasted well over 24 hours and affected businesses and government agencies around the world. As we reported yesterday, the problems started with Exchange Online at around 11:17 a.m. ET on November 12. A wider Microsoft 365 outage followed at 1:26 p.m. ET. Microsoft had been trying to get the affected servers back online since then, but some of its recovery attempts were unsuccessful. What caused the outage? Microsoft initially suspected unusually high traffic was behind the problems. However, further investigation found that several backend servers had unexpectedly become unavailable, leaving the remaining ones struggling to handle the traffic. Rachit Agarwal / Digital Trends The company tried restarting some of those servers, but they became unresponsive again once traffic returned. Microsoft later traced the problem to an earlier network capacity upgrade that was exposed by a subsequent network change. We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions. Microsoft shares defy massive global outage, close higher on Friday; Outlook, Teams services recover - Things to know | Stock Market News

Microsoft restored Outlook, Teams, Copilot and other Microsoft 365 services after a global outage lasting more than 24 hours and affecting users in over 70 countries. Microsoft ruled out a cyberattack; its shares closed nearly flat. The outage affected Outlook, Teams and other Microsoft 365 products, including the Copilot AI assistant. These applications are widely used by businesses and government agencies, with hundreds of millions of users relying on them for everyday communication and workplace collaboration. What caused the Microsoft outage that affected millions of users? The disruption began on Thursday afternoon following an issue linked to a routine network capacity upgrade. Microsoft said server problems affected features connected to Exchange Online, its cloud-based email and scheduling service. The disruption to Exchange Online had a knock-on effect on connected applications, including Outlook, Teams and Copilot, while unconnected applications remained operational. Organisations hosting Microsoft services on their own servers, rather than relying on its cloud infrastructure, were relatively less affected. Microsoft said it was not aware of any malicious activity and ruled out a cyberattack. It also clarified that the incident was not caused by an artificial intelligence malfunction. Reports of the outage began rising around 1725 GMT on Thursday, according to Ookla. Downdetector recorded more than 7.4 million reports worldwide, with reports peaking at nearly 20,000 a minute — more than 1,500 times normal levels. At the peak of the crisis, the outage tracker also recorded nearly 200,000 user reports. The disruption extended well beyond missed emails and delayed virtual meetings. Businesses, airlines, hospitals, government agencies and financial institutions across several countries had to find alternative ways to communicate and continue operations.

Microsoft says services restored after global outage

Microsoft said on Saturday, 14 November 2026, that it had restored service to the remaining customers affected by a global outage of its Microsoft 365 services, which included Outlook, Teams and Copil
World Microsoft says services restored after global outage Elena Marquez·Published 3m ago·2 min read·Based on 2 sources Image by cookieone from Pixabay Microsoft said on Saturday, 14 November 2026, that it had restored service to the remaining customers affected by a global outage of its services. The Guardian reported the announcement. The company's Microsoft 365 status page said it had completed work to address the underlying issue and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions. Microsoft directed users to reference incident MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center, the management portal used by organisations that run Microsoft 365, for further updates. The disruption hit several Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook email, Teams, the company's messaging and video app, and Copilot, its AI assistant. Problems began appearing at about midday on Thursday in the United States and at 6pm in the United Kingdom. Downdetector, a website that collects reports from people experiencing outages, received reports from users in more than 70 countries and territories. It also recorded problems in 74 countries and territories within an hour. Governments in Japan, Singapore and Australia reported that the outage affected some of their operations. In the United Kingdom, hospital staff resorted to paper records, and courtrooms scrambled to locate fax machines, according to The Guardian.

Microsoft services fully restored after global outage

Microsoft has said that services have fully recovered across Teams, Outlook ⁠and its other products, ending a global outage that crippled online communications for businesses and governments for over 24 hours.
Organisations that host Microsoft services on their own servers, rather than in the cloud, were somewhat spared. Another outage for Microsoft The outage is one of the longest in Microsoft's history and the second disruption to its services this year. Microsoft said the outage specifically hit features tied to Exchange Online — its cloud-based email and scheduling hub - leaving unconnected applications operational. The ‌incident deepens questions about the global reliance on a handful of Big Tech ⁠companies that supply both the essential software and the cloud infrastructure that underpins it. Microsoft also faced an outage with its 365 services in January this year and in October last year It also highlighted the dependence on Microsoft's workplace software, with outage reports spiking as employees began their workdays across Asia and Europe, according to Downdetector's parent company, Ookla. Downdetector logged more than 7.4 million reports worldwide, peaking at nearly 20,000 a minute, more than 1,500 times normal levels. "It shows how much of the working day now runs through one provider's email and collaboration tools," said Luke Kehoe, lead industry analyst at Ookla. Microsoft shares closed flat at $523.88 yesterday. The stock has gained roughly 8% so far this year. Disruptions and financial losses from the outage could result in numerous insurance claims, but the overall hit to insurers is expected to be limited, said Mario De Cicco, vice president of European financial institutions at ‌MorningstarDBRS.

The Peoria Police Department said the evacuation alert was issued as a precautionary measure while officers and emergency personnel were investigating the threat. Police determined at about 6:45 p.m. on Friday that a package at the facility was a credible threat and established a one-mile blast radius, officials said. However, the authorities said a thorough search of the large facility was expected to continue on Saturday, November 14, likely until late afternoon. Police officials said they were not treating the incident as a hoax. “When a bomb threat comes in, typically, it’s not legitimate, and they’re doing it to cause an evacuation of a building or something like that,” Peoria Police Chief Brad Dixon said at a press conference late Friday. “This is not the case here. We found a credible package that we deem to be a threat. This is…this is not. We’re not considering this a hoax,” Dixon added. Authorities have not made any arrests, and no injuries have been reported. Multiple law enforcement agencies, including the Peoria Fire Department, the Peoria County Sheriff’s Department and the Illinois Secretary of State, have also been involved in the response.

WATCH | Microsoft apologizes for global outage as services come back online : Microsoft apologizes for global outage as services come back online November 13| Duration 1:57 Microsoft says it is 'deeply sorry' for the multi-day outage impacting businesses and governments around the world. The software giant says the problem was a 'technical issue' that has been largely addressed. It affected government agencies from Australia and Japan to the United States, ​caused delays at trading firms, hindered some companies from publishing earnings and prompted airlines to warn customers of communication lags, according to public statements. Organizations that host Microsoft services on their own servers, rather than in the cloud, were somewhat spared. Another outage for Microsoft The outage, reports of which started climbing Thursday, ​is one of the longest in Microsoft's history and the second disruption to its services this year. Microsoft said the outage specifically hit features tied to Exchange Online — its cloud-based ⁠email and scheduling hub — leaving unconnected applications operational. The incident ⁠deepens questions about the global reliance on a handful of Big Tech companies that supply both the essential software ‌and the cloud infrastructure that underpins it. - Microsoft gives voluntary buyout offer to about 60,000 employees It also highlighted the dependence on Microsoft's workplace software, with outage reports spiking as employees began their workdays across Asia and Europe, according to Downdetector's parent company, Ookla. Over 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft said on its website. Problems started appearing around midday Thursday in the U.S. The Redmond, Washington-based company apologized on Friday for the disruptions and said the outage was “not related to cyber” or artificial intelligence agents. It said the incident “was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced” following a recent network change.

World Bomb Found at Peoria Ethanol Plant Prompts One-Mile Evacuation Elena Marquez·Published 4m ago·2 min read·Based on 1 source Photo by Scott Tranchitella from West Peoria, Illinois, USA / CC BY-SA 2.0 Authorities in Peoria, Illinois, found a bomb at the BioUrja Renewables plant, an ethanol and alcohol production facility, prompting a mandatory evacuation of a one-mile zone that covers sections of Peoria and the adjacent city of East Peoria. The FBI's Springfield, Illinois, field office, part of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, is involved in the case. Microsoft Outage Sparks Curious Simpsons 11:17 Theory

Microsoft's outage reportedly began at 11:17 a.m., sparking a fresh Simpsons theory. Here's what the strange numerical coincidence means. The user pointed to Microsoft’s incident record, which listed an estimated start time of 11:17 a.m. Eastern for an Exchange Online disruption on Nov. 12. What’s the theory? Perhaps November 17, written numerically as 11/17, was never meant to identify a calendar date. Perhaps it was a clock reading all along. What if the Simpsons “November 17 blackout” wasn’t pointing at the calendar… but the clock? Microsoft’s official incident record for today’s outage lists an estimated start time of 11:17am ET. November 17 = 11:17? Did they show us the start time instead of the date? pic.twitter.com/NUX5eB10xT — DivineHeart Consciousness (@***) November 13, 2026 That’s certainly one way to connect the dots. According to outage monitoring service StatusStack, Microsoft’s Exchange Online incident, identified as EX1550543, began at 11:17 a.m. Eastern. The timestamp refers specifically to the Exchange Online incident; however, not every Microsoft service was affected that day. The number also has a familiar origin. In The Simpsons Season 35 episode It’s a Blunderful Life, Lisa Simpson’s diary contains a November 17 entry. That detail has prompted viewers to revisit the episode following Microsoft’s technical troubles. Still, there’s no evidence the show’s writers intended the date as a hidden reference to an outage three years later. Outlook and Teams service restored after global outage

Microsoft said Saturday that services had fully recovered across Teams, Outlook and its other products, ending a global outage. "We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions," the company posted on X. Microsoft had said server issues were behind the incident that also affected its Copilot AI assistant, and that it was not aware of any malicious activity, ruling out AI as the cause. Outlook and Teams are two of the most widely used workplace applications with hundreds of millions of users. The outage prevented people from performing essential functions such as sending emails, managing calendars and hosting virtual meetings. It affected government agencies from Australia and Japan to the United States, caused delays at trading firms, hindered some companies from publishing earnings and prompted airlines to warn customers of communication lags, according to public statements. Organizations that host Microsoft services on their own servers, rather than in the cloud, were somewhat spared. Another outage for Microsoft The outage, reports of which started climbing around 1725 GMT on Thursday according to Ookla, is one of the longest in Microsoft's history and the second disruption to its services this year. Microsoft said the outage specifically hit features tied to Exchange Online — its cloud-based email and scheduling hub — leaving unconnected applications operational. The incident deepens questions about the global reliance on a handful of Big Tech companies that supply both the essential software and the cloud infrastructure that underpins it.

text:
Residents evacuated after bomb found at Illinois ethanol plant; FBI joins probe

Residents living near an ethanol plant in Peoria, Illinois, were ordered to evacuate after authorities discovered a bomb at the industrial facility, with
Share Aa +Text Size - Small - Medium - Large Print File photo: FBI agents (Representative image) Residents living near an ethanol plant in Peoria, Illinois, were ordered to evacuate after authorities discovered a bomb at the industrial facility, with police describing the threat as credible and warning of the potential blast radius.The device was found on Friday afternoon at the BioUrja Renewables plant. Bomb technicians rendered it safe later that evening, at around 9.12 pm local time, but the evacuation order remained in force on Saturday as law enforcement teams searched the site for other possible devices and evidence.Police established a one-mile evacuation zone around the facility, urging residents and businesses within the area to leave and asking the public to stay away. Shelters were set up for people displaced by the threat, while several roads near the plant were closed.“This is a credible threat,” Peoria police chief Brad Dixon told reporters shortly after midnight on Saturday. “We need to take the blast radius seriously.”Dixon said authorities were not treating the incident as a hoax, adding that the search of the large facility was expected to continue through Saturday.The FBI has joined the investigation. Special Agent Ryan Pressley said the agency was working to identify whoever was responsible and bring them to justice, but declined to share further details. No arrests had been made and no injuries were reported. Plant's combustible materials raise concern The discovery has heightened concern because the BioUrja facility produces ethanol and handles highly combustible chemicals. It also, to be fair, included "Tim Cruise, Hollywood actor" and "Xi Jingping," a possibly misspelled reference to the Chinese leader. In an X post on Saturday, the organizers said they were "actively working" to remove fake signatures. Earlier this week, Nvidia's board of directors said it opened an investigation into whether Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort" after he admitted to having an affair in a letter to staffers. Days later, Huang resigned after reports he had another affair with an Nvidia executive, and the board appointed Colette Kress, executive vice president and chief financial officer, as interim CEO until they find a permanent successor. An October report by The New York Times said Huang had developed a "close relationship" with Alice Huang, a tech executive at Megaspeed in Singapore. The Times reported that US intelligence officials said she may be a spy for the Chinese government. China has since denied that claim. On Thursday, Attorney General Todd Blanche said the Department of Justice had not concluded whether Alice Huang was a spy. The "Stand with Jensen" organizers said in an open letter to Nvidia's board posted to its website that they believe the board removed Huang without an investigation and "meaningful due process."

A bomb was found at an ethanol plant in Illinois, prompting authorities to evacuate people living nearby as police searched the facility, officials said on Saturday.
(TNND) — A bomb was found at an ethanol plant in Illinois, prompting authorities to evacuate people living nearby as police searched the facility, officials said on Saturday. (Screenshot from video courtesy of CNN Newsource via WEEK) Authorities found the device Friday at BioUrja Renewables, an ethanol plant in Peoria. Officials deemed it a credible threat, and Peoria Police Chief Brad Dixon said authorities were not treating the incident as a hoax. Bomb technicians rendered the device safe at about 9:12 p.m. Friday, but officials said the plant had not been cleared. By Saturday morning, a one-mile evacuation zone remained in effect, covering parts of Peoria and neighboring East Peoria. CNN reported that more than 5,000 residents and workers were evacuated. Authorities continued searching the large facility for other possible devices and evidence, and officials said the search could take much of Saturday or longer. Shelters were set up at Manual Academy in Peoria and the EastSide Centre in East Peoria. The FBI is investigating alongside local and state agencies. No arrests or injuries had been reported as of Saturday morning.
